title: Effects of Indoor Lighting (Illuminance and Spectral Distribution) on the Performance of Cognitive Tasks and Interpersonal Behaviors: The Potential Mediating Role of Positive Affect
research_question: To investigate the impact of illuminance and spectral distribution on a wide range of nonvisual work-related tasks, and to determine whether these effects can be understood in terms of the mediating role of positive affect.

participants.description: Undergraduate students (male and female) enrolled in introductory psychology at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, USA.
participants.recruitment: Voluntary participation to fulfill a course requirement.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A specially prepared experimental room (3.22m x 3.35m x 2.45m) with off-white walls and ceiling, and a light-blocking drape over the window. Lighting was provided by four-lamp recessed fluorescent luminaries with flat prismatic lenses. Temperature and humidity were held constant.

Illuminance levels: approximately 150 lux (low) or 1500 lux (high) on the desk surface. Varied by increasing or reducing the number of lamps lit. Lamps were new and operated for 100 hours to stabilize. (Study 1, 2, 3)
Lamp types (spectral distribution): warm white (3000K), natural white (3600K), cool white (4200K), and Design 50 (D50, 5000K). Varied by changing lamps in ceiling fixtures. (Study 1)
Lamp types (spectral distribution): warm white or cool white fluorescent bulbs. (Study 2, 3)
Small, unexpected gift (several pieces of candy in a plastic bag) given to subjects in the 'gift' condition. (Study 3)

measures.instrument: Ratings of a fictitious employee on 9 dimensions (qualifications, skills, competence, motivation, performance, ability to get along, intelligence, hiring recommendation, overall rating) on 7-point scales.
Ratings of exemplars for 4 categories (vehicle, furniture, clothing, vegetable) on a 10-point scale (extent of belonging). Focus on nontypical exemplars.
Positive Affect-Negative Affect Scale (PANAS; Watson et al., 1988), 5-point scales.
Ratings on dimensions like unattractive-attractive, pleasant-unpleasant, like-dislike, dim-bright, colorless-colorful, glare-nonglare, clear-hazy.
Current Feelings Survey (10 dimensions like sad-happy, anxious-calm, sleepy-awake) on 7-point scales.
Thomas-Kilmann MODE Scale (avoidance, compromise, collaboration, accommodation, competition).
Self-set goal (number of items for clerical task), confidence in goal, perceived ability to perform, expected effort (7-point scales).
Number of items completed in a 5-minute clerical coding task.
Likelihood ratings (7-point scales) of 5 courses of action (compromise, accommodation, competition, avoidance, collaboration) in response to a co-worker's failure, under 3 causal explanations.
Ratings of similarity of experimental room lighting to home, offices, restaurants, classrooms, stores.
Amount of time (minutes) subjects were willing to volunteer for extra, unpaid tasks.

findings.consequent: Performance appraisals of a fictitious employee (job-related skills, competence, motivation, hiring recommendation, overall rating)
findings.mechanism: Hypothesized to be mediated by positive affect, as positive affect has been shown to increase favorable evaluations.
findings.quote: subjects rated the employee significantly higher on several different dimensions [e.g., secretarial skill, competence, overall hiring recommenda- tion in the low-illuminance (150 lux) condition than in the high-illuminance (1500 lux) condition (p < .05 in all cases)].

findings.antecedent: Low illuminance (150 lux) with warm-white or natural-white lamps
findings.consequent: Inclusion of nontypical exemplars as category members (word categorization task)
findings.mechanism: Hypothesized to be mediated by positive affect, as positive affect has been shown to increase the assignment of nontypical exemplars.
findings.quote: subjects in the low-illuminance condition generally assigned higher ratings to the poor ex- emplars than those in the high-illuminance condition.

findings.consequent: Performance appraisals (not qualified-qualified, responsible-irresponsible)
findings.mechanism: Cool-white light seemed to counter or reduce the positive effects induced by low levels of illuminance.
findings.quote: for all lamp types except the cool white, ratings were higher in the low-illuminance than in the high-illuminance con- dition. This pattern was reversed for the cool-white condition.

findings.consequent: Perceived relaxing quality of the room
findings.mechanism: Direct affective reaction to spectral distribution.
findings.quote: subjects in the cool-white condition rated the room as less relaxing (M = 4.27) than those exposed to the other three lamps (M = 3.09, 3.05, 3.41, respectively, for the warm-white, natural-white, and D50 bulbs)

findings.consequent: Perceived pleasantness of the room
findings.mechanism: Direct affective reaction to spectral distribution.
findings.quote: subjects rated the room as being more pleasant in the warm-white condition and as being least pleasant in the cool-white condi- tion

findings.consequent: Perceived glare of the room
findings.mechanism: Direct visual comfort effect.
findings.quote: Subjects in the warm-white condition also evaluated the room as less glaring (M = 5.50) than those in the D50 con- dition [M = 4.05;

findings.consequent: Positive and Negative Affect Scale (PANAS) scores
findings.mechanism: PANAS may not be sensitive enough or shifts were too subtle for self-report.
findings.quote: No significant effects emerged from these overall analyses. Thus, there was no evidence, on scores for this measure, that subjects experienced differential affective reactions to the various lighting conditions.

findings.consequent: Self-reported feelings of anxious-calm
findings.mechanism: Lighting conditions influencing positive affect.
findings.quote: Subjects reported being more calm and more awake in the 150-lux than in the 1500-lux condition (refer to Table III).

findings.consequent: Self-reported feelings of sleepy-awake
findings.mechanism: Lighting conditions influencing positive affect and/or arousal.
findings.quote: Subjects reported being more calm and more awake in the 150-lux than in the 1500-lux condition (refer to Table III).

findings.consequent: Tendencies to resolve interpersonal conflicts through collaboration (MODE Scale)
findings.mechanism: Hypothesized to be mediated by positive affect, as positive affect enhances collaborative conflict resolution.
findings.quote: subjects reported stronger tendencies to resolve interpersonal conflicts through collaboration in the warm-white (M = 6.63) than in the cool-white condition (M = 5.31).

findings.consequent: Tendencies to resolve interpersonal conflicts through avoidance (MODE Scale)
findings.mechanism: Hypothesized to be mediated by positive affect, as positive affect reduces avoidance in conflict resolution.
findings.quote: subjects reported weaker tendencies to resolve interpersonal con- flicts through avoidance in the warm-white (M = 5.55) than in the cool- white (M = 7.17) condition.

findings.consequent: Tendency to resolve interpersonal conflicts through avoidance (MODE Scale)
findings.mechanism: Combined effect of warm-white and low illuminance on positive affect, leading to reduced avoidance.
findings.quote: the warm white-low illuminance group differed significantly from all the others; subjects in this group reported the weakest tendency to resolve conflicts through avoidance (M = 4.67).

findings.consequent: Self-reported ability to perform a clerical coding task
findings.mechanism: Hypothesized to be mediated by positive affect, as positive affect increases confidence in one's abilities.
findings.quote: in the warm- white condition, subjects reported significantly higher ability in the low-il- luminance than in the high-illuminance condition (M = 6.06 vs. 5.28, p < .05).

findings.consequent: Perceived brightness of the room
findings.quote: subjects rated the high- illuminance condition as brighter and more clear than the low-il- luminance condition.

findings.consequent: Perceived clarity of the room
findings.quote: subjects rated the high- illuminance condition as brighter and more clear than the low-il- luminance condition.

findings.consequent: Perceived glare of the room
findings.quote: Subjects rated the room as more glaring in the high-illuminance than in the low-illuminance condition.

findings.consequent: Perceived similarity of lighting to home and restaurants
findings.mechanism: Familiarity with lighting conditions in different settings.
findings.quote: subjects in the low-illuminance condition rated lighting in the experimental room as more similar to that in their homes and in restaurants than did subjects in the high-illuminance condition.

findings.consequent: Perceived similarity of lighting to business offices and hospitals
findings.mechanism: Familiarity with lighting conditions in different settings.
findings.quote: subjects in the high-illuminance condition rated lighting in the experimental room as more similar to businesses offices and hospitals than did subjects in the low-illuminance condition

findings.antecedent: Receipt of a small, unexpected gift
findings.consequent: Self-reported positive feelings (Current Feelings Survey Factor 1)
findings.mechanism: Known to induce positive affect.
findings.quote: individuals who received a gift reported more positive feelings (factor 1) and greater activation or alertness (factor 2) than those who did not receive a gift.

findings.antecedent: Receipt of a small, unexpected gift
findings.consequent: Self-reported activation or alertness (Current Feelings Survey Factor 2)
findings.mechanism: Known to induce positive affect and arousal.
findings.quote: individuals who received a gift reported more positive feelings (factor 1) and greater activation or alertness (factor 2) than those who did not receive a gift.

findings.antecedent: Warm-white, low-illuminance lighting (in absence of gift)
findings.consequent: Self-reported feelings of calmer and more relaxed (Current Feelings Survey Factor 3)
findings.mechanism: Lighting conditions influencing positive affect (calmness/relaxation).
findings.quote: among subjects who did not receive a gift, those exposed to warm-white light reported feeling significantly calmer and more relaxed in the low-illuminance than in the high-illuminance condition.

findings.consequent: Performance appraisals of a fictitious employee
findings.mechanism: Hypothesized to be mediated by positive affect, replicating Study 1 findings.
findings.quote: subjects as- signed higher ratings to the imaginary employee in the low-illuminance (M =- 4.86) than in the high-illuminance condition (M = 3.71).

findings.antecedent: Receipt of a small, unexpected gift
findings.consequent: Performance appraisals (deserves merit raise, deserves promotion)
findings.mechanism: Known to induce positive affect, leading to more favorable evaluations.
findings.quote: subjects who had received a small gift rated the employee higher on both dimensions than those who had not received a gift

findings.consequent: Amount of time volunteered for extra tasks
findings.mechanism: Hypothesized to be mediated by positive affect, as positive affect increases helping behavior.
findings.quote: subjects exposed to warm-white light volunteered more time (M = 19.51 min) than those exposed to cool-white light (M = 14.17 min).

findings.antecedent: Receipt of a small, unexpected gift
findings.consequent: Amount of time volunteered for extra tasks
findings.mechanism: Known to induce positive affect, increasing willingness to help.
findings.quote: participants who received a gift (M = 18.98) volunteered more time than those who did not (M = 14.71).

findings.antecedent: Low illuminance (150 lux) (in absence of gift)
findings.consequent: Amount of time volunteered for extra tasks
findings.mechanism: Modest increments in positive affect induced by low levels of illuminance increased helping behavior. This effect was eliminated by the presence of a gift (ceiling effect).
findings.quote: in the absence of a gift, subjects in the 150-lux condition donated more time (M = 17.90) than those in the 1500-lux condition (M = 11.53).

mechanisms: Positive affect: Lighting conditions (low illuminance, warm-white light) induce positive affect, which in turn influences cognition and behavior (e.g., evaluations, categorization, conflict resolution, helping).
Arousal: Variations in illuminance and color may induce shifts in arousal, which could influence behavior.
Priming of specific memories or memory categories: Environmental cues might prime certain cognitive associations.
Familiarity: Relative familiarity with various lighting conditions may influence affective reactions.
moderators: Receipt of a small, unexpected gift
Apparent cause of conflict (ambiguous, external, internal)
implementation_implications: Indoor lighting can influence work-related behaviors beyond visual tasks, suggesting its importance for employee well-being and productivity.
Low illuminance and warm-white light may foster positive affect, leading to more favorable evaluations, broader thinking, and prosocial behaviors like collaboration and helping.
Designers should consider both illuminance and spectral distribution for their non-visual impacts on occupants' mood and social interactions.

limitations: Findings were obtained under restricted laboratory conditions and relatively short duration, limiting generalizability to actual work settings.

The PANAS measure did not yield significant effects, suggesting it may not be sensitive enough to detect subtle environmentally induced shifts in affect, or that such shifts were too small for self-report.
Only two levels of illuminance were employed, making it difficult to determine the precise dose-response relationship or optimal levels.
The study employed a between-subjects design, which might limit participants' capacity to monitor and verbally describe subtle shifts in affective states.
The potential mediating role of arousal was not fully explored and needs further investigation.
The possibility of a ceiling effect for positive affect when a gift was present might have masked lighting effects on helping behavior.
Relative familiarity with various lighting conditions (e.g., office vs. home lighting) might play a role in affective reactions, which was not fully accounted for.
